main.title: Cannon Spike
main.subtitle: Capcom characters in an arena of fire
main.summary: Cannon Spike is Psikyo's multidirectional arena shooter, released in arcades in 2000 and on Dreamcast later that year.

cards.heading: Capcom characters in an arena of fire
cards.text: Cannon Spike is Psikyo's multidirectional arena shooter, released in arcades in 2000 and on Dreamcast later that year. Capcom characters including Cammy, Charlie and Arthur fight through concentrated encounters with a strong emphasis on bosses. The player moves around the arena while shooting and striking nearby opponents, with a second player able to join. The crossover provides recognizable faces, but the immediate problem is spatial: keep the character away from danger while maintaining an effective attack on a moving target.

cards.heading: Mark a target and keep moving
cards.text: A Mark command locks onto an opponent, separating the choice of target from the direction of movement. Shooting handles distant enemies, while a close-range attack can push back or damage something that gets too near. Combining buttons produces additional ranged and melee specials. A stronger super attack requires a Special Token, making its use a limited resource. These commands give a short encounter several possible responses, from circling a marked boss to clearing the immediate space with a forceful nearby strike.

cards.heading: A small crossover built around bosses
cards.text: The seven-character roster reaches across Capcom's games, with Mega Man and Baby Bonnie Hood among the hidden choices. The international title takes its name from Cammy's familiar attack. Psikyo's arcade experience concentrates that collection of characters into brisk stages and boss fights rather than a long narrative journey. The NAOMI arcade hardware made Dreamcast a natural home for the conversion, whose North American release arrived in November 2000. Its appeal comes from seeing familiar characters translated into another studio's shooting vocabulary.

main.title: Donald Duck: Goin’ Quackers
main.subtitle: A temper made for platform games
main.summary: Released in 2000 and known in Europe as Quack Attack, Ubisoft’s adventure sends Donald after Merlock, who has kidnapped the reporter Daisy. Gyro Gearloose’s laboratory connects the journey’s different worlds, while Gladstone provides a rival in the rescue. Jumping, fighting and collecting objects turn Donald’s cartoon impatience into a platform game. The original Nintendo 64 manual explicitly describes his changing moods: taking a hit affects his temperament, making his familiar eruptions of anger part of the action rather than just a cutscene gag.

cards.heading: One name, several versions
cards.text: The Windows, Dreamcast and Nintendo 64 editions were developed by Ubi Soft Casablanca, with music by Daniel Masson. The PlayStation edition has its own production team and Shawn K. Clément's score; Clément also composed for the PlayStation 2 version and its later GameCube edition. Different teams adapted Donald's adventure to each machine, changing the layouts, presentation and music across its releases.

main.title: The Operative: No One Lives Forever
main.summary: The Operative: No One Lives Forever (abbreviated as NOLF) is a first-person shooter video game developed by Monolith Productions and published by Fox Interactive, released for Windows in 2000.

cards.text: The Operative: No One Lives Forever (abbreviated as NOLF) is a first-person shooter video game developed by Monolith Productions and published by Fox Interactive, released for Windows in 2000. The game was ported to the PlayStation 2 and Mac OS X in 2002.

A story-driven game set in the 1960s, No One Lives Forever received critical acclaim for its stylistic representation of the era in the spirit of many spy films and television series of that decade, as well as for its humor. Players control female protagonist Cate Archer, who works for a secret organization that watches over world peace. In addition to a range of firearms, the game contains several gadgets disguised as ordinary female fashion items.

At the time of its release, many reviewers considered No One Lives Forever one of the best first-person shooters since 1998's Half-Life. After receiving several Game of the Year awards in the press, a special Game of the Year Edition was released in 2001, which included an additional mission on a remote island in the South Pacific. The Operative: No One Lives Forever was followed by a sequel, No One Lives Forever 2: A Spy in H.A.R.M.'s Way, in 2002, and a spin-off titled Contract J.A.C.K. released in 2003, both developed by Monolith.

A re-release of the game has been hampered by the complicated state of the series' intellectual property (IP) rights, with even parties assumed to be in possession of the IP having publicly admitted not knowing the precise legal situation of the series.

main.title: Summon Night
main.subtitle: Tactics by day, bonds by night
main.summary: Flight-Plan and Banpresto bring tactical battles and nightly conversations together on PlayStation.

cards.heading: Tactics by day, bonds by night
cards.text: Summon Night debuted on PlayStation in Japan on January 6, 2000. Flight-Plan and Banpresto built its strategy RPG around adventure scenes, tactical encounters and nightly conversations with companions. Summoning and positioning shape the battles, while conversations develop relationships between them. The alternating structure established a mixture that later entries would continue to explore.

cards.heading: Chapters move between companions and combat
cards.text: Each chapter moves through adventure scenes, battles and conversations. A party of up to eight units fights on tactical maps, carrying familiar characters from the story into combat. Between encounters, talking to companions gives them space outside their battlefield roles. The chapter structure keeps these meetings close to the decisions about whom to deploy.

cards.heading: Position and summoning
cards.text: Height, distance and attack direction influence positioning, alongside the abilities of individual units. Summonite Stones add preparation through the creatures and effects they allow a summoner to call. Choosing a summon and finding a useful place to use it become connected decisions, giving the game's fantasy a direct role in its tactical rules.

cards.heading: Conversations after the battle
cards.text: Nightly conversations let the player spend time with a chosen companion after major events. These exchanges develop personal relationships alongside the wider journey. Together with the adventure and battle phases, they give each chapter a distinct closing moment: a chance to return to someone in the party and learn more about them.

main.title: Resident Evil – Code: Veronica
main.summary: Resident Evil – Code: Veronica is a 2000 survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom for the Dreamcast.

cards.heading: Resident Evil – Code: Veronica
cards.text: Resident Evil – Code: Veronica is a 2000 survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom for the Dreamcast. It was the first Resident Evil game to debut on a platform other than PlayStation. The story takes place three months after the events of Resident Evil 2 (1998) and the concurrent destruction of Raccoon City as seen in Resident Evil 3: Nemesis (1999). It follows Claire Redfield and her brother Chris Redfield in their efforts to survive a viral outbreak at a remote prison island in the Southern Ocean and a research facility in Antarctica. The game retains the series' traditional controls and gameplay; however, unlike the pre-rendered backgrounds of previous installments, Code: Veronica uses real-time 3D environments and dynamic camera movement.

cards.heading: Claire enters European gothic horror
cards.text: After producer Shinji Mikami and his team learned they would be unable to port Resident Evil 2 to the Sega Saturn, they began development on an original game, which became Code: Veronica. Claire was designed with a tougher appearance than in Resident Evil 2, with the reason being her past experiences in Raccoon City built her toughness and confidence. Unlike the American horror themes and settings of previous games in the series, Code: Veronica employs a European gothic horror design and settings. This is achieved through the use of gothic architecture and gothic art in addition to the writing style and story presentation.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: Capcom announced Code: Veronica in August 1998 and released it in February 2000 after delays and a reduction in sales expectations due to the struggling Dreamcast platform. Sales were weak compared to other Resident Evil games, but strong compared to other Dreamcast games. Code Veronica received critical acclaim and has been considered among both the best Resident Evil games and Dreamcast games. In 2001, Capcom released an updated version on Dreamcast and PlayStation 2, Code: Veronica X. The revised version included new cutscenes which revealed more details about the story, and it was ported to the GameCube in addition to other platforms in later years. In September 2011, Capcom released a high-definition remastered version of Code: Veronica X for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. Code: Veronica was adapted for Capcom's Gun Survivor series with Resident Evil Survivor 2 – Code: Veronica (2002) and also later adapted for Resident Evil: The Darkside Chronicles (2009). A remake, Resident Evil Veronica, is scheduled for release in 2027.

main.title: The Sims
main.subtitle: A household with a life of its own
main.summary: Maxis found play in relationships, rooms and the small disruptions of a household.

cards.heading: Daily life becomes the game
cards.text: Released for Windows in North America on February 4, 2000, The Sims builds a game around the daily life of a household. Will Wright and Maxis turn rooms, objects, jobs and relationships into connected systems. Players build and furnish a home, then direct inhabitants who also act on their own. A kitchen, a friendship or enough time to sleep can become the centre of a story.

cards.heading: From architecture to inhabitants
cards.text: Wright's interest in architecture helped shape the project. Christopher Alexander's A Pattern Language suggested ways to think about how people use space, while SimAnt offered experience with agents responding to signals and priorities. Early inhabitants were intended to reveal whether a house worked. As the prototypes developed, their behaviour became the focus, with architecture providing the setting for a social simulation.

cards.heading: Objects invite behaviour
cards.text: A bed relieves fatigue, a refrigerator answers hunger and a shower restores hygiene. Sims evaluate these possibilities and may act autonomously while the player rearranges their priorities. Wright recalled that the team reduced the effectiveness of this autonomy: self-sufficient inhabitants left players too little to do. Furnishing a house therefore means shaping behaviour as well as choosing its appearance, with accidents and delays keeping plans unsettled.

cards.heading: Stories across ordinary days
cards.text: Work, money, mood and friendships supply a continuing set of goals across successive days. Players can build towards a personal ambition or follow a situation that emerges in the household. The Strong inducted The Sims into its World Video Game Hall of Fame in 2016, highlighting its role in broadening the audience for games. Its domestic setting made building, observation and personal storytelling central pleasures of play.

main.title: Vagrant Story
main.subtitle: Lea Monde as a Narrative Machine
main.summary: Vagrant Story follows Ashley Riot into Leá Monde, a ruined city caught in a struggle over religious and political power.

cards.heading: A city under suspicion
cards.text: Vagrant Story follows Ashley Riot into Leá Monde, a ruined city caught in a struggle over religious and political power. Square released the PlayStation game in 2000. Its enclosed streets, cellars and stone chambers place a solitary investigator inside a city that rarely offers a straightforward route or explanation.

cards.heading: Choose where to strike
cards.text: Combat pauses while Ashley selects an enemy body part within his weapon's reach. Timed follow-up attacks extend a chain, but raise Risk. Continuing an attack can therefore make the next exchange less safe. The system asks for both a tactical choice before the blow and a rhythmic response after it.

cards.heading: Prepare the weapon
cards.text: Weapons develop different strengths against different enemy classes, and workshops allow equipment to be combined and adjusted. A disappointing hit can be a reason to reconsider the weapon rather than simply repeat the attack. Preparation makes the city's next locked room or unfamiliar creature a practical problem as well as a mystery.

main.title: Ridge Racer 64
main.summary: Ridge Racer 64 is a 2000 racing video game developed by Nintendo Software Technology and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64.

cards.heading: Ridge Racer 64
cards.text: Ridge Racer 64 is a 2000 racing video game developed by Nintendo Software Technology and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo 64. It is the first title of Namco's Ridge Racer series to not be on arcades or a PlayStation console, with Namco licensing the series to Nintendo to develop the game. In 2004, the game was remade for the Nintendo DS as Ridge Racer DS, which uses the system's features such as the touch-screen and wireless multi-player. Additionally, Gina Cavalli from R: Racing Evolution replaced Reiko Nagase as the mascot in the DS version. The N64 version received its first official re-release on the Nintendo Classics service on January 31, 2025; followed by a Japanese release on May 16, 2025.

main.title: Fear Effect
main.subtitle: Three mercenaries follow a dangerous lead
main.summary: Fear Effect is Kronos Digital Entertainment's PlayStation action-adventure, first released in North America on 24 February 2000. Set in Hong Kong in 2050, it follows Hana, Glas and Deke through a story that moves from criminal intrigue towards supernatural horror. The player alternates between its protagonists, combining exploration, combat and puzzles. Its illustrated characters stand against moving backgrounds, giving the scenes a distinctive animated appearance. The presentation makes each location feel like part of a continuous film while the player remains responsible for finding a route through its dangers.

cards.heading: Three mercenaries follow a dangerous lead
cards.text: Fear Effect is Kronos Digital Entertainment's PlayStation action-adventure, first released in North America on 24 February 2000. Set in Hong Kong in 2050, it follows Hana, Glas and Deke through a story that moves from criminal intrigue towards supernatural horror. The player alternates between its protagonists, combining exploration, combat and puzzles. Its illustrated characters stand against moving backgrounds, giving the scenes a distinctive animated appearance. The presentation makes each location feel like part of a continuous film while the player remains responsible for finding a route through its dangers.

cards.heading: The background keeps moving
cards.text: Fear Effect uses streaming or looping full-motion video for its environments rather than relying only on still pre-rendered scenes. Characters move within these animated spaces, where a fixed view can conceal both an object needed for a puzzle and a threat approaching the player. Combat and stealth share time with investigation, making the next scene more than a place to shoot. The player must understand what the camera reveals and what the situation requires. This mixture gives the adventure a deliberate pace, interrupted by sudden demands for action.

cards.heading: An illustrated thriller across four discs
cards.text: The video-based presentation helped spread the original release across four PlayStation discs. Matt Furniss and Jason Agolia supplied its music, while the visual treatment of the characters anticipated techniques that became more common in later games. Reviews generally praised its cinematic character and distinctive appearance, with difficulty a frequent reservation. Fear Effect 2: Retro Helix followed as a prequel in 2001. The original's identity remains closely tied to the contrast between readable, illustrated figures and backgrounds that continue to move around them, supporting a thriller that changes its direction as it unfolds.

main.title: PlayStation 2
main.subtitle: DVD and the Emotion Engine take PlayStation into a new generation
main.summary: PlayStation 2 launched in Japan on 4 March 2000, followed by North America and Europe later that year.

cards.heading: One machine, several roles
cards.text: PlayStation 2 launched in Japan on 4 March 2000, followed by North America and Europe later that year. Its DVD drive carried new games and could also play films. For a living room, the purchase could introduce a new game console and a DVD player at the same time.

cards.heading: Keep the earlier collection
cards.text: Compatibility with original PlayStation discs let many existing games remain useful on the new console. Players could bring their previous collection into the new generation alongside games developed for the Emotion Engine. That continuity made the original PlayStation library part of the new machine's appeal.

cards.heading: Games and accessories expand the system
cards.text: Network play and the EyeToy camera expanded the console's uses during its lifetime. Different games and accessories brought these possibilities into living rooms over the following years, alongside the growing DVD-based library. The machine that began as a new PlayStation and a film player gradually supported a broader range of activities.

sources.title: PlayStation 2 reaches 50 million units
sources.supports: The retrospective press release states Japan March 4, 2000; North America October 26; Europe/PAL November 24.

cards.heading: Planning the chips' journey
cards.text: Sony's 1999 annual report introduced the next PlayStation through two central chips: the Emotion Engine and Graphics Synthesizer. It also described how those chips would be made. Plans for the Emotion Engine involved a venture with Toshiba and production lines at Oita, while Graphics Synthesizer manufacturing required another facility at Nagasaki. The promised world on a television depended on industrial work far from the living room. These investments prepared the console for production in large numbers.

cards.heading: An investment before a picture
cards.text: The report linked those planned facilities to ambitions for expressive characters, moving clothing and compatibility with existing PlayStation software. Its proposals capture the scale of Sony's investment before release. Developers would have to turn the architecture and its promises into working scenes, building tools suited to their own games.

cards.heading: Moving a world through memory
cards.text: Stephen White's 2002 Jak and Daxter postmortem describes one such production problem. Naughty Dog wanted connected environments without stopping at obvious loading boundaries. Designers had to arrange areas so they could enter and leave memory unobtrusively. Programmers built processing tools and several forms of detail reduction; artists followed specialised construction rules while supplying large amounts of content. A landscape visible in the distance was therefore a joint technical and artistic task. Studios had to decide what should remain in memory at each moment.

cards.heading: Changing code while it runs
cards.text: The studio's GOAL language offered another way to make that work practical. White explained that programmers could compile and download changes while the game continued running, seeing the effect without restarting it. His account also records the cost: support and fixes depended heavily on one programmer, creating a bottleneck. The tool could speed an experiment while making the team dependent on its maintenance. That tension belongs beside a console's specifications. Production capacity includes how quickly people can test an idea, understand a failure and keep working together.
